automotive-001.question: In AEC-Q100, the reliability qualification standard for automotive ICs, which ambient temperature range is specified for operating temperature Grade 1?
automotive-001.explanation: AEC-Q100 grades denote ambient temperature ranges; the smaller the number, the higher the upper limit. Grade 0 is −40 to 150 °C, Grade 1 is −40 to 125 °C, Grade 2 is −40 to 105 °C and Grade 3 is −40 to 85 °C. −40 to 150 °C is the most stringent, Grade 0, and −40 to 85 °C is the Grade 3 range. Because self-heating makes the chip's junction temperature higher than the ambient temperature, thermal design must also account for that difference.

automotive-002.question: Which correctly pairs AEC-Q100, AEC-Q101 and AEC-Q200, the qualification standards for automotive electronic components, with the components they mainly cover?
choices: Q100: integrated circuits (ICs); Q101: discrete semiconductors such as diodes and transistors; Q200: passive components such as resistors and capacitors
Q100: passive components; Q101: integrated circuits (ICs); Q200: discrete semiconductors such as diodes and transistors
Q100: discrete semiconductors; Q101: passive components; Q200: integrated circuits (ICs)
automotive-002.explanation: The AEC standards are divided by component type. Integrated circuits such as microcontrollers and power ICs fall under AEC-Q100; discrete semiconductors such as diodes, power MOSFETs and IGBTs fall under AEC-Q101; and passive components such as resistors, capacitors, inductors and crystal resonators fall under AEC-Q200. Because the components differ in structure and failure behavior, the test items and conditions also differ. For example, automotive multilayer ceramic capacitors use AEC-Q200-compliant types.

automotive-003.question: Assume an automotive component operates continuously 24 hours a day for 15 years. Approximately how many hours is its total operating time?
choices: About 13,000 hours
About 1,300,000 hours
About 130,000 hours
automotive-003.explanation: A year is about 8,760 hours, so 15 years is 8,760 × 15 = 131,400 hours, or about 130,000 hours. Electronic components in passenger cars are often designed around a service life of about 15 years, requiring longer lifetimes than consumer equipment. However, for a car driven 2 hours a day, driving time over 15 years comes to only about 11,000 hours. Operating time differs by an order of magnitude depending on whether the component also operates while parked or charging, so it is important to define concrete usage conditions when setting test conditions.

automotive-004.question: Which best describes the "zero defect" philosophy required for automotive semiconductors?
choices: Since a certain percentage of defects is unavoidable, assume that parts failing in the field will be replaced free of charge with new ones and that the cost will be covered by warranty
Strict 100% inspection before shipment is sufficient, so no particular effort is needed in design or process control
Targeting zero defects, prevent defects from being built in and escaping at every stage of design, manufacturing and test, and identify the cause of even a single defect to prevent recurrence
automotive-004.explanation: Car failures can endanger lives, and a single vehicle uses thousands of semiconductors, so the defect rate per component must be extremely low. Zero defect is a philosophy that targets zero defects and combines design margin, process control and testing that removes outlier chips to prevent defects from being built in and escaping. If even one defect occurs in the field, the root cause is analyzed and used to prevent recurrence. Inspection alone still lets defects slip through, so design and process control are also essential.

automotive-005.question: Which correctly describes PPAP (Production Part Approval Process) used in the automotive industry?
choices: A procedure for demonstrating to the customer, with documents and samples, that parts made with the same processes, equipment and conditions as mass production meet requirements, and obtaining approval
A procedure for filing new circuit ideas as patents at the prototype stage to secure the rights
A procedure for compiling the number of field failures and the failure rate every month after shipment and reporting them to the customer together with an improvement plan
automotive-005.explanation: PPAP (Production Part Approval Process) is a procedure in which a supplier, before starting mass production, demonstrates that parts made with the same processes, equipment and conditions as mass production meet customer requirements and can be produced consistently, and obtains approval. Submissions include design records, process FMEA, control plan, dimensional and characteristic measurement results, process capability studies and samples. The approved process becomes the baseline for mass production, so changing the process later requires notifying the customer. It is separate from patent filing or field failure reporting.

automotive-006.question: For an automotive semiconductor, which is the correct way to proceed when you want to change the manufacturing fab or the materials used?
choices: If internal checks confirm the electrical characteristics are within the datasheet specifications, the change can be made without informing the customer
Notify the customer in advance of the change and its impact via a PCN (Product Change Notification), present requalification results as needed, and obtain agreement
The customer only needs to be informed if a problem occurs in the field after the change
automotive-006.explanation: Automotive components are premised on being made with the approved design, process and fab. Changing the fab, materials, process or package can alter reliability or subtle characteristics even if values stay within the datasheet. Therefore, the change and its impact are notified in advance via a PCN (Product Change Notification), the necessary reliability tests are repeated, and the switch is made after obtaining the customer's agreement. AEC-Q100 also gives guidelines on which tests to repeat for each type of change.

automotive-007.question: What is the main purpose of recording the lot number, wafer number and on-wafer coordinates during wafer test in electrically programmable non-volatile memory (such as fuses) inside an automotive IC?
choices: To use chip-unique values as encryption keys and encrypt all communication on the in-vehicle network to prevent eavesdropping
To record the temperature of the operating chip and control it so it does not overheat
To identify the lot, wafer and position of a returned failed chip and cross-reference it with manufacturing and test records
automotive-007.explanation: Once a chip is sealed in a package, you cannot tell from outside which wafer it came from or where on the wafer it was. If identification data is written into the chip, it can be read out when a failed part is returned from the field, tracing back to manufacturing conditions and even wafer test measurements. It also helps narrow down which other products processed on the same equipment might be affected. This is chip-level traceability. Encryption keys generally use a separate dedicated mechanism that is hard to read out.

automotive-008.question: In qualification of automotive ICs, what is the main reason HAST (a biased test in pressurized water vapor at around 130 °C and 85% RH) is sometimes used instead of the temperature humidity bias test (THB) run at 85 °C and 85% RH for 1000 hours?
choices: It accelerates failures such as corrosion caused by moisture ingress, shortening a 1000-hour test to around 100 hours
It allows evaluation of soft errors caused by cosmic rays instead of moisture-induced failures
Raising the temperature drives out moisture, allowing lifetime to be evaluated in a dry state
automotive-008.explanation: HAST (Highly Accelerated Stress Test) is a method that tests at temperatures above 100 °C under pressure while maintaining high humidity. Raising the temperature and water vapor pressure speeds the movement of moisture through the package mold compound to the chip, accelerating electrode corrosion, increased leakage current and similar failures. For example, it is common to run about 96 hours at 130 °C and 85% RH as an evaluation equivalent to 1000 hours at 85 °C and 85% RH. It has nothing to do with evaluating soft errors or dry conditions.

automotive-009.question: Why are latch-up tests on automotive ICs required to be performed at the product's maximum operating temperature, which is more severe than room temperature?
choices: Because parasitic transistors become less active at higher temperatures, making latch-up less likely, so the test can be run under conditions that are easier to pass
Because at higher temperatures the current gain of the parasitic transistors and the well resistance increase, making latch-up more likely
Because ESD protection circuits stop working at high temperature, so the ESD test can be completed at the same time
automotive-009.explanation: CMOS latch-up is a phenomenon in which parasitic pnp and npn transistors conduct as a thyristor and a large current keeps flowing. As temperature rises, the current gain of the parasitic transistors increases and the well and substrate resistance also increases, so even a small current can trigger conduction. Therefore, under AEC-Q100, tests that inject current into pins or apply overvoltage are performed as JESD78 Class II conditions at the maximum operating temperature set by the temperature grade (ambient; for example, 125 °C for Grade 1). High temperature is not used to relax the conditions, and the test is performed separately from ESD tests.

automotive-010.question: Which correctly describes the difference between component-level ESD tests of ICs, such as HBM (human body model) and CDM, and system-level ESD tests performed on finished automotive equipment?
choices: The two use the same conditions, so if the IC passes the component-level test, no protection components need to be added to the equipment's board
Component-level tests assume handling during manufacturing and assembly, while system-level tests assume cases such as a person touching the equipment in use, with much higher discharge energy
System-level tests have lower discharge energy, so they are always easier to pass than component-level tests
automotive-010.explanation: HBM (human body model) and CDM (charged device model) are tests that assume static electricity when ICs are handled in controlled factories; a rating of around 2 kV in the human body model, for example, is one common target. System-level tests, which assume discharges such as from a person touching a door or switch, use high voltages from a few kV to more than 10 kV (up to about 25 kV for air discharge), with much higher discharge energy. The IC's internal protection circuits alone often cannot withstand this, so protection components such as TVS diodes are added on the board at externally connected pins.

automotive-011.question: Which correctly describes the functional safety standard ISO 26262?
choices: A standard for reducing hazards caused by failures of electrical and electronic systems in series-production road vehicles, adapted for automotive use from IEC 61508
A standard covering occupant protection in a collision, such as body crash strength and airbag deployment performance
An internationally harmonized standard for quality management systems at automotive parts plants, adding automotive-industry-specific requirements to ISO 9001
automotive-011.explanation: ISO 26262 is a functional safety standard for reducing to an acceptable level the risk that a vehicle behaves hazardously due to failures of electrical and electronic systems. It adapts IEC 61508, the basic functional safety standard for electrical/electronic/programmable electronic systems, to automotive use and covers the entire lifecycle from concept through development, production and decommissioning. Crash safety concerns body and airbag performance and is addressed by other requirements. The automotive standard for quality management is IATF 16949.

automotive-012.question: Which correctly describes the concept of automotive functional safety?
choices: Using only high-quality components to bring the component failure rate to zero, guaranteeing that no failure of any kind ever occurs during the vehicle's service life
Designing the vehicle so that accidents never occur no matter what incorrect operation the driver performs
Not eliminating failures, but reducing risk to an acceptable level, for example by detecting failures when they occur and transitioning to a safe state
automotive-012.explanation: Since component failures cannot be eliminated completely, functional safety aims to prevent a hazardous situation when a failure occurs. For example, if an anomaly is detected in the motor control of electric power steering, assist is stopped, a warning lamp notifies the driver, and the system moves to a state in which the driver can steer manually. ISO 26262 defines functional safety as the absence of unreasonable risk due to hazards caused by malfunctioning behavior of E/E systems. It does not guarantee that accidents will never happen.

automotive-013.question: In ISO 26262, which correctly lists the three factors evaluated when determining the ASIL through hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA)?
choices: Severity (S), exposure (E), controllability (C)
Failure rate (λ), diagnostic coverage (DC), fault tolerant time interval (FTTI)
Component price, production volume, development period
automotive-013.explanation: The ASIL is determined for each hazardous event by evaluating three factors: severity S, representing how serious the injuries are; exposure E, representing the frequency or duration of exposure to driving situations in which the hazard can occur; and controllability C, representing how likely the driver or others are to avoid the hazard. For example, sudden loss of braking at high speed has high severity and is hard to avoid, so it receives a high ASIL. Failure rate, diagnostic coverage and FTTI are quantities used after the ASIL is determined, to evaluate whether a design meets its requirements.

automotive-014.question: Which correctly describes the ASIL in ISO 26262?
choices: It ranges from A to D, with ASIL A representing the most stringent requirements. QM represents even more stringent requirements than ASIL D
It ranges from A to D, with ASIL D representing the most stringent requirements. When the risk is sufficiently low, the classification is QM and it is handled by ordinary quality management
It ranges from A to D, with ASIL D representing the components with the highest failure rate. QM represents components with no quality issues, for which all testing may be skipped
automotive-014.explanation: ASIL (Automotive Safety Integrity Level) has four levels, A, B, C and D, with D the most stringent, imposing high requirements on development processes, safety mechanisms, failure rate targets and so on. For example, parts of airbag, brake and steering control are typical cases that often require ASIL D. When the risk is low and no ASIL needs to be assigned, the classification is QM (Quality Management) and development is carried out under ordinary quality management. Quality still has to be assured under QM, and testing cannot be skipped.

automotive-015.question: A hazardous event was assessed as severity S3, exposure E4 and controllability C3, giving ASIL D. If, for the same event, only controllability were C2 (most drivers can normally avoid the hazard), what would the ASIL be?
choices: ASIL D
ASIL B
ASIL C
automotive-015.explanation: In the ISO 26262 ASIL table, only the combination S3, E4, C3 gives ASIL D; lowering any one of S, E or C by one level lowers the ASIL by one level to ASIL C. As a handy rule of thumb, if the sum of the S number (1–3), E number (1–4) and C number (1–3) is 10 it is D, 9 is C, 8 is B, 7 is A, and anything lower is QM. In this example, 3 + 4 + 2 = 9, so it is ASIL C. It neither stays at ASIL D nor drops two levels.

automotive-016.question: Which correctly describes a "safety goal" in ISO 26262?
choices: A top-level safety requirement determined from the results of hazard analysis and risk assessment, expressed for example as "do not cause unintended sudden acceleration," and assigned an ASIL
A target number of safety-related tests to be performed within a development project, where more tests are judged to mean higher safety
A target failure-rate value set for each component, independent of ASIL, with the same value used for all components
automotive-016.explanation: A safety goal is a top-level safety requirement defined at the vehicle level to prevent a hazardous event identified in HARA. For electronic throttle control, for example, it is expressed as "do not cause unintended sudden acceleration," and it inherits the ASIL of that hazardous event. The safety goal is broken down step by step into functional safety requirements, technical safety requirements, and hardware and software requirements. It is neither a target number of tests nor a uniform failure-rate value unrelated to ASIL.

automotive-017.question: Which correctly pairs the descriptions of random hardware failures and systematic failures as distinguished in ISO 26262?
choices: Random hardware failures occur probabilistically during use due to degradation, cosmic rays and so on, while systematic failures occur under specific conditions because of causes such as specification or design errors
Random hardware failures occur under specific conditions because of specification or design errors, while systematic failures occur probabilistically during use
Random hardware failures occur only in software, while systematic failures occur only in hardware
automotive-017.explanation: Random hardware failures, such as component degradation or bit flips from cosmic rays, are failures whose occurrence can be predicted only probabilistically; they are evaluated quantitatively with failure rates (FIT) using metrics such as SPFM and PMHF. Systematic failures are caused by missing requirements, design errors, software bugs and the like, and always recur when the same conditions are met. These are not evaluated probabilistically but prevented through development processes such as reviews and verification appropriate to the ASIL. Hardware design errors are also systematic failures.

automotive-018.question: For PMHF, the metric for the probability that a safety goal is violated due to random hardware failures, the target guideline for ASIL D is less than 10 FIT. What is this expressed as a probability per hour?
automotive-018.explanation: 1 FIT is one failure per 10⁹ hours, or 1×10⁻⁹ /h. Therefore 10 FIT is 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 1×10⁻⁸ /h. PMHF (Probabilistic Metric for random Hardware Failures) is the probability per hour, averaged over the vehicle's service life, that a safety goal is violated due to random hardware failures. Target guidelines are less than 100 FIT (10⁻⁷ /h) for ASIL B and C, and less than 10 FIT for ASIL D.

automotive-019.question: Which is the correct target guideline for the single-point fault metric (SPFM) required for ASIL D?
choices: 90% or higher
60% or higher
99% or higher
automotive-019.explanation: SPFM indicates how few of the safety-related faults are single-point faults, which by themselves lead to violation of a safety goal, or residual faults, which remain undetected by safety mechanisms; it is calculated as 1 minus the proportion of their combined failure rate. Target guidelines are 90% or higher for ASIL B, 97% or higher for ASIL C and 99% or higher for ASIL D. The latent fault metric (LFM) guidelines are 60% or higher for ASIL B, 80% or higher for ASIL C and 90% or higher for ASIL D, so 90% and 60% are easily confused with LFM or ASIL B values.

automotive-020.question: Which is the most appropriate example of a latent fault in ISO 26262?
choices: A fault that, occurring alone, cannot be detected or controlled even by safety mechanisms and immediately leads to violation of a safety goal
A state in which the ECC correction circuit is broken, but nothing happens as long as no memory error occurs, so it remains unnoticed
A fault that was detected by a safety mechanism and reported to the driver with a warning lamp
automotive-020.explanation: A latent fault is a fault that is not hazardous by itself and remains unnoticed by both safety mechanisms and the driver. For example, even if the correction circuit of the ECC, a safety mechanism, is broken, it does not show up as long as there are no memory errors. If a bit error then occurs in memory, it is not corrected and can lead to a hazard. Because a hazard arises only when two faults coincide, the latent fault metric (LFM) evaluates how small the proportion of latent faults is. A fault that immediately becomes hazardous is a single-point fault, and a detected fault is not a latent fault.

automotive-021.question: The total failure rate of safety-related hardware is 1000 FIT, of which single-point faults and residual faults (faults that remain undetected by safety mechanisms) total 5 FIT. What is the single-point fault metric (SPFM)?
automotive-021.explanation: SPFM is calculated as 1 minus the "sum of the single-point and residual fault failure rates" divided by the "total safety-related failure rate." In this example, 1 − 5 / 1000 = 1 − 0.005 = 0.995, or 99.5%. This meets the ASIL D guideline of 99% or higher. 95% is the value obtained by overestimating the proportion by an order of magnitude, and 99.95% by underestimating it by an order of magnitude. To raise SPFM, add safety mechanisms with high diagnostic coverage to reduce faults that remain undetected.

automotive-022.question: A safety mechanism with 99% diagnostic coverage is added to a circuit with a failure rate of 200 FIT. What is the failure rate of the faults that remain undetected by the safety mechanism?
choices: 198 FIT
0.02 FIT
2 FIT
automotive-022.explanation: Diagnostic coverage (DC) is the proportion of faults that a safety mechanism can detect or control. The remaining failure rate is 200 × (1 − 0.99) = 200 × 0.01 = 2 FIT. 198 FIT is the failure rate of the faults the safety mechanism can detect, and 0.02 FIT is the result of misplacing the decimal point in the multiplication. Fault coverage in manufacturing test represents the proportion of defective parts found before shipment, whereas diagnostic coverage represents the proportion of faults occurring in use that are detected on the spot.

automotive-023.question: Which correctly describes the fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) in ISO 26262?
choices: The average time a component can be used without failing; it has the same meaning as MTTF, and longer means safer
The time from a fault occurring until repair is completed; shorter is considered safer
The minimum time from a fault occurring until a hazardous event could occur if no countermeasure were taken; fault detection and transition to a safe state must be completed within this time
automotive-023.explanation: FTTI is the minimum time from the occurrence of a fault until a hazardous event would occur if safety mechanisms did not act. A safety mechanism must keep the sum of the time to detect the fault and the time from detection to reaching a safe state, for example by shutting off outputs, within the FTTI. For example, for a function with an FTTI of several tens of ms, a diagnosis once every few seconds is too slow. It is a different concept from MTTF, which represents component life, or from repair time.

automotive-024.question: Which correctly describes how a lockstep CPU, used as a safety mechanism in automotive microcontrollers, works?
choices: Two CPU cores share different tasks between them, roughly doubling processing speed
Two CPU cores execute the same instructions simultaneously, and their outputs are compared every clock cycle; a mismatch is reported as a fault
When a fault is detected, CPU operation is temporarily stopped (locked), switched to a spare circuit, and the faulty part is automatically repaired before resuming
automotive-024.explanation: Lockstep is a scheme in which two identically configured CPU cores run the same program and a comparator checks their outputs against each other. If one result changes due to a bit flip from cosmic rays or a circuit fault, it is detected as a mismatch, giving high diagnostic coverage for CPU faults. Because the two cores do the same work, performance equals that of one core. Comparing two cores alone cannot tell which one is correct, so after detection the system performs a reset or a transition to a safe state.

automotive-025.question: What is the main reason for offsetting the execution of the two cores in a lockstep CPU by a few clock cycles, or placing the two cores apart on the chip?
choices: If the same cause, such as supply noise or radiation, produces the same error in both cores at the same time, the comparison cannot detect it, so this makes identical errors less likely
So that one core can use the other core's computation results in advance, speeding up processing
So that the two cores can each run different programs, increasing the number of usable cores
automotive-025.explanation: Lockstep detects faults through differences between the two cores' results, so it cannot detect identical errors produced in both by the same cause. Such failures are called common cause failures. Momentary supply voltage drops or clock disturbances affect both cores simultaneously, so delaying one core's execution by, for example, 2 clock cycles and realigning the results for comparison makes it less likely that the same error occurs at the same timing. Placing the cores apart likewise keeps localized causes from affecting both.

automotive-026.question: An automotive microcontroller's memory uses ECC (SEC-DED), which can correct 1-bit errors and detect 2-bit errors. What generally happens when read data contains a 2-bit error?
choices: Errors of up to 2 bits are automatically corrected using the check bits, so no error is reported and processing continues as is
The error can be neither detected nor corrected, so the erroneous data is used and processing continues
It cannot be corrected but can be detected, so an error is reported and actions such as moving the system to a safe state are taken
automotive-026.explanation: SEC-DED (Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection) adds, for example, 8 check bits to 64 bits of data, correcting 1-bit errors and reliably detecting 2-bit errors, although it cannot correct them. When a 2-bit error is detected, the microcontroller reports the error, and software does not use the data and performs a reset or a transition to a safe state. Recording 1-bit errors as well, after correcting them, makes it possible to catch signs of trouble before errors accumulate.

automotive-027.question: Which correctly describes a feature of a window watchdog timer?
choices: Once kicked, it stops monitoring to reduce power consumption
It detects as an anomaly not only kicks (timer clears) that come too late relative to a defined time window but also kicks that come too early
When a kick is late, it assumes the program is doing heavy processing and, without resetting, automatically extends the wait time to let processing continue
automotive-027.explanation: An ordinary watchdog issues a reset if it is not kicked within a certain time. However, in anomalies where the program skips part of its processing and runs in a short loop, kicks arrive early and may go unnoticed. A window watchdog defines a time window in which kicking is allowed and treats kicks that are too early or too late as anomalies. In automotive systems, the watchdog is sometimes placed in an external monitoring IC running on a clock separate from the microcontroller, so that a common cause does not stop both.

automotive-028.question: What is the main functional safety purpose of running logic BIST and memory BIST in an automotive microcontroller at power-up or before driving?
choices: To find latent faults that do not show up in normal operation, such as those in the safety mechanisms themselves, and raise the latent fault metric (LFM)
To skip pre-shipment testing at the factory and eliminate test costs
To automatically raise the CPU operating frequency and speed up processing while driving
automotive-028.explanation: Even if safety mechanisms such as the ECC correction circuit or comparators are broken, this does not show up in normal operation, so such faults remain latent. Testing the chip's own circuits with logic BIST and memory BIST at power-up finds such faults before driving and raises the LFM. Running BIST takes time, during which normal processing cannot be done, so the design must also consider startup time constraints. It is not a replacement for shipment testing or a means of speeding up processing.

automotive-029.question: Which is an appropriate clock-monitoring safety mechanism for an automotive microcontroller?
choices: Use a separate oscillator independent of the main clock as a reference to detect stoppage or frequency deviation of the main clock
Use a reference derived from the main clock itself to measure the frequency of that same main clock
Set the clock frequency higher than specified so that processing finishes in time even if a failure occurs
automotive-029.explanation: If the clock stops or its frequency drifts, timer intervals and communication speeds go wrong and control can no longer be performed correctly. Therefore, the clock period is counted against a separate reference independent of the main clock, such as an internal oscillator, and an anomaly is reported if it falls outside a defined range. With a reference derived from the same clock being monitored, monitoring stops when that clock stops, so the anomaly cannot be found. Setting the frequency above specification actually causes malfunctions.

automotive-030.question: Which is an appropriate voltage-monitoring safety mechanism provided in functional-safety-compliant automotive power ICs and similar devices?
choices: Only drops in supply voltage need to be monitored; rises do not affect microcontroller operation or lifetime, so they need not be monitored
Deriving the monitoring circuit's reference voltage from the same reference as the monitored supply reduces part count and therefore also improves safety
Use a reference voltage independent of the monitored supply, and detect not only when the supply voltage falls below the allowable range but also when it exceeds it (overvoltage)
automotive-030.explanation: When the microcontroller's supply voltage drops, timing is not met and it malfunctions; when it rises too high, it leads to malfunction or to degradation and destruction of devices. Therefore, voltage monitoring as a safety mechanism detects both undervoltage and overvoltage and, on an anomaly, resets the microcontroller or shuts off outputs. If the reference voltage is shared with the monitored supply, a reference shift moves the supply and the monitor in the same way and the anomaly is missed, so an independent reference is used. A typical brownout detector (BOD), which resets only when voltage drops, cannot meet this requirement on its own.

automotive-031.question: In ISO 26262 ASIL decomposition, which combination is permitted for splitting an ASIL D safety requirement and allocating it to two sufficiently independent redundant elements?
choices: ASIL A(D) and ASIL A(D)
ASIL B(D) and ASIL B(D)
QM(D) and QM(D)
automotive-031.explanation: In ASIL decomposition, the same safety requirement can be allocated at lower ASILs to mutually independent redundant elements. The permitted decompositions of ASIL D are B(D) and B(D), C(D) and A(D), and D(D) and QM(D). The (D) in parentheses indicates the original ASIL. A dependent failure analysis must show that the two elements will not fail simultaneously from the same cause. Also, the targets for the random hardware failure metrics remain those of the original ASIL D even after decomposition.

automotive-032.question: Which correctly describes SEooC (Safety Element out of Context) in ISO 26262?
choices: A component used only in non-safety-related applications, to which ISO 26262 need not be applied; an IC for car audio is an example
A device installed outside the vehicle, on roads or traffic signals, that communicates with vehicles to support safety; a roadside communication unit is an example

An element developed before the target system is determined by assuming its usage and higher-level safety requirements, with the user verifying those assumptions; a general-purpose automotive microcontroller is an example
automotive-032.explanation: General-purpose automotive microcontrollers and power ICs are developed before it is known which system of which vehicle they will be used in. So the semiconductor manufacturer develops them by assuming safety requirements and usage (for example, "used together with an external watchdog"), and provides those assumptions and how to use the safety mechanisms in a safety manual. This is SEooC. The developer of the system using the component confirms that those assumptions hold in their design. It does not mean a component exempt from ISO 26262.

automotive-033.question: Which correctly describes FMEDA (Failure Modes, Effects and Diagnostic Analysis) performed in functional safety assessment?
choices: Tabulating, for each part of a circuit, the failure modes and failure rates, their effects and the proportion detectable by safety mechanisms, and calculating SPFM, LFM and other metrics
Analyzing the delay of each circuit path to find the maximum clock frequency at which the chip can operate
Compiling the uptime and failure records of each piece of manufacturing equipment to estimate the fab's production capacity and the number of additional tools needed for mass production
automotive-033.explanation: FMEDA is FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) with a diagnostic perspective added. For each part, such as memory, CPU, clock and power supply, failure rates and failure modes such as stuck-at faults and malfunctions are assigned, and the analysis summarizes whether each leads to violation of a safety goal and which safety mechanisms detect how much of it. From the results, SPFM, LFM and PMHF are calculated, and safety mechanisms are added if the targets are not met. Failure rate values are derived from failure rate handbooks, test data and so on.

automotive-034.question: When the functions of multiple ECUs are integrated into a single high-performance SoC and software of different ASILs runs together, which is required?
choices: Place the lower-ASIL and higher-ASIL software in the same memory region and let them read and write data freely
Isolate them with memory protection, timing monitoring and similar measures so that malfunctions of lower-ASIL software do not encroach on the memory or execution time of higher-ASIL software
Give the lower-ASIL software higher priority and run the higher-ASIL software only in idle time
automotive-034.explanation: Consolidating multiple functions in one SoC reduces the number of components and ECUs, but bugs in lower-ASIL software may interfere with higher-ASIL functions by corrupting memory or using up CPU time. Therefore, freedom from interference is demonstrated through spatial partitioning with memory protection units or a hypervisor, and temporal partitioning by allocating and monitoring execution time. Without partitioning, everything must be developed to the highest ASIL, which requires much more effort.

automotive-035.question: In CAN, what happens when two nodes start transmitting frames at the same time?
choices: The two frames collide and both are corrupted, so both nodes wait a random time before retransmitting
The frame with the smaller ID value (higher priority) continues transmitting and the losing node stops and retransmits later, so the winning frame is not corrupted
The frame with the larger ID value takes priority, and the frame with the smaller ID value is discarded and not retransmitted
automotive-035.explanation: On a CAN bus, when 0 (dominant) and 1 (recessive) are driven simultaneously, 0 wins. A transmitting node compares each bit it sends with the bus state and, if it sent a 1 but sees a 0, judges that it has lost arbitration and stops transmitting. Since the ID is sent first, smaller ID values have higher priority, and the winning frame arrives intact. This is called non-destructive arbitration. Waiting a random time after a collision is the CSMA/CD method of early Ethernet.

automotive-036.question: On a CAN bus with 120 Ω termination resistors at both ends, the resistance between CAN_H and CAN_L was measured with the power off. Which value is closest to that of a normal bus?
automotive-036.explanation: A CAN bus has a 120 Ω termination resistor at each end to prevent signal reflections. Seen from between CAN_H and CAN_L, the two 120 Ω resistors are in parallel, giving 120 × 120 / (120 + 120) = 60 Ω. A reading of 120 Ω suggests one termination resistor is missing, and around 40 Ω suggests a wiring error such as three termination resistors being fitted. 240 Ω is the mistake of treating the two as being in series.

automotive-037.question: Which correctly describes a feature of CAN FD?
choices: Arbitration is performed at the same speed as conventional CAN, only the data phase switches to a faster bit rate, and up to 64 bytes can be sent per frame
It uses optical fiber instead of copper wire to send the same maximum of 8 bytes of data as conventional CAN at higher speed
It eliminates arbitration and divides time into slots, switching to a time-triggered scheme in which each node's transmission time is predetermined, making it much faster
automotive-037.explanation: Conventional CAN (Classical CAN) runs at up to 1 Mbit/s with up to 8 bytes of data per frame. CAN FD performs the arbitration phase, in which all nodes must see the bits aligned, at the conventional speed and switches only the data phase to a speed of several Mbit/s. Data length also increases to up to 64 bytes, making software reprogramming and sensor data transmission more efficient. It does not use optical fiber, and the time-triggered scheme is a feature of FlexRay.

automotive-038.question: Which correctly describes a feature of the in-vehicle network LIN?
choices: A high-speed scheme communicating at up to 10 Mbit/s over two differential signal lines, used for safety-critical control such as braking and steering
A scheme communicating at 1 Gbit/s over a single twisted pair, used to transmit camera video and display data
A low-speed (up to about 20 kbit/s) and inexpensive scheme connecting one master and multiple slaves on a single signal wire, used for controlling power windows, mirrors and the like
automotive-038.explanation: LIN (Local Interconnect Network) uses a single signal wire and has slaves transmit in an order determined by the master; it is slow, up to about 20 kbit/s. It can be built with simple communication circuits similar to a UART, and slaves can synchronize without a high-precision oscillator, making it inexpensive. It connects parts that do not need speed, such as power windows, mirrors, seats and switches, as a subnetwork of CAN. The 10 Mbit/s scheme describes FlexRay, and the 1 Gbit/s scheme describes automotive Ethernet.

automotive-039.question: Which correctly describes a feature of the in-vehicle network FlexRay?
choices: An event-triggered scheme in which nodes contend for the right to transmit by ID priority, communicating inexpensively over a single signal wire at up to 20 kbit/s
A time-triggered scheme that divides time into slots and has each ECU transmit at a predetermined time; a redundant configuration using two channels of up to 10 Mbit/s each is also possible
A scheme that superimposes communication signals on power lines, eliminating signal wiring and making the vehicle lighter
automotive-039.explanation: FlexRay is a time-triggered scheme that pre-assigns time slots for each ECU's transmission within the communication cycle, and is characterized by deterministic data delivery times. It runs at up to 10 Mbit/s per channel and can use two channels to send the same data in a redundant configuration, so it has been used for chassis control and similar applications. Contending for the right to transmit by ID is a feature of CAN, and a 20 kbit/s single wire is a feature of LIN. In new designs, migration to automotive Ethernet is also under way.

automotive-040.question: Which correctly describes a feature of automotive Ethernet (100BASE-T1, 1000BASE-T1, etc.)?
choices: It communicates full-duplex over a single twisted pair, providing 100 Mbit/s or 1 Gbit/s of bandwidth while keeping wiring light
The standard mandates the same four-pair cables and RJ45 connectors as office LANs, making the wiring heavier than in offices
Its communication speed is about the same as LIN, but because it is robust against noise it is used only for safety-critical control
automotive-040.explanation: Automotive Ethernet standards such as 100BASE-T1 and 1000BASE-T1 communicate full-duplex over just a single twisted pair, are lighter than the four-pair cables used in offices, and also cope with harsh automotive noise conditions. With far greater bandwidth than CAN, they are used for camera and display data, the backbone network linking ECUs, software reprogramming and more. Time synchronization and latency guarantees are achieved by combining TSN (Time-Sensitive Networking) technologies.

automotive-041.question: Which correctly describes the ongoing shift to a "zonal architecture" in automotive electronic systems?
choices: A configuration that keeps adding dedicated ECUs for each function, such as engine, brakes and navigation, further increasing the number of ECUs
A configuration that connects all of the vehicle's electronic components in series on a single wire and controls them without using any ECUs

Consolidating the wiring of sensors and actuators and power distribution into zone ECUs placed in each location (zone) of the vehicle, and linking them to a high-performance central computer over a high-speed network
automotive-041.explanation: Traditionally, each added function brought another dedicated ECU, leading to more than 100 ECUs in some luxury cars along with long, heavy wiring harnesses. In a zonal architecture, zone ECUs in each location, such as the front, rear, left and right of the vehicle, connect nearby sensors and actuators, while control processing is consolidated in a high-performance central computer. Wiring becomes shorter and lighter, and batch software updates become easier. Zone ECUs also handle power distribution, replacing fuses and relays with semiconductor switches.

automotive-042.question: Which is the appropriate approach when performing an OTA (Over-the-Air) update, which rewrites vehicle software wirelessly?
choices: Perform updates while driving whenever possible and, to avoid disturbing the driver, switch automatically to the new software version without notification before the driver notices
Verify the software's digital signature to prevent tampering, apply the update in a safe state such as while parked, and make it possible to roll back to the previous version if the update fails
Skip digital signature verification because it takes time, and perform the update prioritizing download speed
automotive-042.explanation: OTA updates allow features to be added and bugs to be fixed without a dealer visit, but if counterfeit software is installed, control of the vehicle could be hijacked. Therefore, a digital signature is used to verify that the software comes from the legitimate distributor. Updates are applied with the driver's consent at a time that does not affect driving, such as while parked, and the vehicle can still boot the previous version if the update fails. In some regions, cybersecurity and software update management systems based on UN regulations (UN R155 and R156) are required.

automotive-043.question: Which correctly describes the difference between the automotive standards ISO 26262 and ISO/SAE 21434?
choices: ISO 26262 addresses hazards caused by component failures and design errors, while ISO/SAE 21434 addresses protection against threats from malicious attacks (cyberattacks)
ISO 26262 addresses protection against threats from cyberattacks, while ISO/SAE 21434 addresses hazards caused by component failures and design errors
The two have the same content; ISO/SAE 21434 is the new number assigned when ISO 26262 was revised
automotive-043.explanation: ISO 26262 is a functional safety standard for preventing hazards caused by random hardware failures and systematic failures, evaluating risk through HARA. ISO/SAE 21434 is a cybersecurity standard for protecting vehicles from intentional attacks such as hijacking communications or tampering with software, evaluated through threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA). Their scopes differ, but if an attack disables safety mechanisms, safety is also compromised, so the two activities are carried out in coordination.

automotive-044.question: When the same power is delivered through wiring of the same resistance, by roughly what factor does the Joule loss in the wiring change if the supply voltage is raised from 12 V to 48 V?
automotive-044.explanation: Since power P = VI, for the same power, quadrupling the voltage reduces the current to 1/4. Wiring loss is I²R, so it becomes (1/4)² = 1/16. For example, delivering 2.4 kW requires 200 A at 12 V but 50 A at 48 V. 48 V systems are used in mild hybrids, electric auxiliaries and the like, allowing thinner, lighter wiring. Staying at or below 60 V is another advantage, since it does not require the rigorous electric-shock protection of high-voltage systems. 1/4× is the current ratio, not the loss ratio.

automotive-045.question: Which voltage class is commonly used for the power devices in the traction inverter of an electric vehicle with an 800 V battery?
choices: 650 V class
100 V class
1200 V class
automotive-045.explanation: Power devices see not only the supply voltage itself but also voltage variations with state of charge and surge voltages during switching, so a breakdown voltage with margin is required. Devices in the 650–750 V class are commonly used for 400 V systems and the 1200 V class for 800 V systems, and SiC MOSFETs, which have low losses even at high breakdown voltages, are increasingly adopted. Moving to 800 V halves the current for the same power compared with 400 V, making it easier to raise fast-charging power and allowing thinner cables. The 650 V class is the guideline for 400 V systems.

automotive-046.question: Which correctly describes "load dump," a problem in automotive power supplies?
choices: A phenomenon in which a large current flows into the starter motor at engine start, causing the battery voltage to drop sharply
A phenomenon in which the battery is disconnected while the alternator (generator) is charging, producing a large surge voltage on the supply line
A phenomenon in which lightning strikes the vehicle body and a large current flows into the supply line, destroying components
automotive-046.explanation: Load dump is a phenomenon in which the battery is disconnected, for example by a terminal coming loose, while the generator is charging at high current, and the energy with nowhere to go makes the supply line voltage spike. Even in a 12 V system, without suppression circuitry it can reach close to 100 V as a rough guide and last for tens to hundreds of ms (40–400 ms for 12 V systems in ISO 16750-2 Test A). In vehicles that limit the voltage on the generator side (Test B), it is clamped to about 35 V, so many ICs connected directly to the battery have a voltage rating of about 40 V or more, and they are further protected with TVS diodes and similar devices. The voltage drop at engine start is a different phenomenon called cranking.

automotive-047.question: Which best describes how IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs and GaN HEMTs are chosen for power conversion in electrified vehicles?
choices: GaN HEMTs are superior at every voltage, so it is common to replace everything with GaN, including 1200 V class traction inverters
IGBTs switch the fastest, so they are best suited to small DC-DC converters operating at high frequencies in the MHz range

Si IGBTs and SiC MOSFETs are used for high-voltage, high-current traction inverters, while GaN is increasingly adopted in on-board chargers and DC-DC converters that are made smaller by using high frequencies
automotive-047.explanation: IGBTs handle high voltage and high current at low cost, but tail current at turn-off makes them unsuitable for high frequencies. SiC MOSFETs have low losses even in the 1200 V class and are increasingly adopted in applications such as 800 V traction inverters. GaN HEMTs excel at particularly fast switching at the 650 V class and below, and are beginning to be used in on-board chargers and DC-DC converters where higher frequencies are wanted to shrink components. It is important to choose for each application by comparing material properties and cost.

automotive-048.question: Which correctly describes a feature of millimeter-wave radar used in ADAS (advanced driver assistance systems)?
choices: It uses radio waves in the 76–81 GHz band, its performance degrades little in rain, fog or at night, and it can directly measure relative velocity via the Doppler effect
It excels at distinguishing color and shape and is best suited for reading the text on road signs and the colors of traffic lights
It scans the surroundings finely with laser light and can measure object shapes as fine 3D point clouds with the highest resolution of any automotive sensor
automotive-048.explanation: Millimeter-wave radar uses reflections of radio waves to measure the distance and direction to objects, and can also directly obtain relative velocity from the frequency shift of the reflected wave (Doppler effect). Radio waves are little affected by rain, fog or darkness, so radar is widely used for functions such as maintaining the gap to the vehicle ahead. On the other hand, its angular resolution is low, and it is poor at classifying object types. Recognizing colors and text is the strength of cameras, and high-resolution 3D point clouds are the strength of LiDAR; sensor fusion combines them so each compensates for the others' weaknesses.

automotive-049.question: A LiDAR takes 400 ns from emitting a laser pulse until the reflected light returns from an object. Approximately how far away is the object? (speed of light 3×10⁸ m/s)
automotive-049.explanation: Light travels to the object and back, so distance is speed of light × time ÷ 2. 3×10⁸ m/s × 400×10⁻⁹ s = 120 m is the round-trip distance, so the one-way distance is 60 m. 120 m is the value obtained by forgetting to divide by 2. Measuring distance from the round-trip time of light in this way is called ToF (Time of Flight). LiDAR can measure 3D shapes with high resolution, but its performance tends to degrade in dense fog or heavy rain as light scatters, and cost is also a challenge.

automotive-050.question: Which of the following problems is addressed mainly by SOTIF (ISO 21448, Safety of the Intended Functionality) rather than ISO 26262 (functional safety)?
choices: A component in the radar transmitter circuit degrades and fails after years of use under stresses such as temperature changes, so objects ahead can no longer be detected
Because of an error in the brake control software, the braking force is miscalculated under specific conditions
A camera that has not failed cannot recognize a pedestrian ahead due to strong backlight, and automatic emergency braking does not activate
automotive-050.explanation: SOTIF addresses hazards that arise even when no component has failed, from sensor performance limitations, insufficient recognition algorithms, inadequate specifications, foreseeable misuse and the like. Failing to recognize a pedestrian in backlight is a problem caused not by a failure but by a functional limitation, so it falls under SOTIF. Failure due to component degradation is a random hardware failure and a software error is a systematic failure; both are handled by ISO 26262. In SOTIF, testing and simulation are used to reduce unknown hazardous scenarios.
